title: Envelope encryption: a data key locks the data, and a key in KMS locks the data key
captions: To save a record, your app makes a new data encryption key (DEK). It encrypts the data with the DEK, for example with AES-256-GCM.
The app sends the DEK to KMS. KMS encrypts it, or wraps it, with the key encryption key (KEK). The KEK never leaves KMS.
The app stores the ciphertext next to the wrapped DEK. It never stores the plain DEK. A new DEK for each write means DEKs do not need rotation.
To read, the app sends the wrapped DEK to KMS. KMS checks the caller's permission, unwraps the DEK and sends it back. The app decrypts the data.
A copy of the database holds only ciphertext and wrapped DEKs. To unwrap them, an attacker must call KMS with your permissions. The plain DEK in memory is still a weak point.
